evidence: This is presented as a known perception among researchers.

claim: The benefits of open practices outweigh the potential costs.
source: In the present article, we address such concerns and suggest that the benefits of open practices outweigh the potential costs.
evidence: This is the main argument of the manuscript, to be supported by the evidence presented.

claim: Publishing openly is associated with higher citation rates.
source: There is evidence that publishing openly is associated with higher citation rates (Hitchcock, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hitchcock, 2016.

claim: Articles published in PNAS under their open access option were twice as likely to be cited within 4–10 months than non-OA articles published in the same journal.
source: For example, Eysenbach reported that articles published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) under their open access (OA) option were twice as likely to be cited within 4–10 months and nearly three times as likely to be cited 10–16 months after publication than non-OA articles published in the same journal (Eysenbach, 2006).
evidence: This is a specific finding from Eysenbach, 2006.

claim: Articles published in PNAS under their open access option were nearly three times as likely to be cited 10–16 months after publication than non-OA articles published in the same journal.
source: For example, Eysenbach reported that articles published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) under their open access (OA) option were twice as likely to be cited within 4–10 months and nearly three times as likely to be cited 10–16 months after publication than non-OA articles published in the same journal (Eysenbach, 2006).
evidence: This is a specific finding from Eysenbach, 2006.

claim: Hajjem and colleagues studied over 1.3 million articles published in 10 different disciplines over a 12-year period.
source: Hajjem and colleagues studied over 1.3 million articles published in 10 different disciplines over a 12-year period and found that OA articles had a 36–172% advantage in citations over non-OA articles (Hajjem et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the study design from Hajjem et al., 2006.

claim: OA articles had a 36–172% advantage in citations over non-OA articles across 10 disciplines over 12 years.
source: Hajjem and colleagues studied over 1.3 million articles published in 10 different disciplines over a 12-year period and found that OA articles had a 36–172% advantage in citations over non-OA articles (Hajjem et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from Hajjem et al., 2006.

claim: Some controlled studies have failed to find a difference in citations between OA and non-OA articles.
source: While some controlled studies have failed to find a difference in citations between OA and non-OA articles or attribute differences to factors other than access (Davis, 2011; Davis et al., 2008; Frandsen, 2009a; Gaulé and Maystre, 2011; Lansingh and Carter, 2009), a larger number of studies confirm the OA citation advantage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davis, 2011; Davis et al., 2008; Frandsen, 2009a; Gaulé and Maystre, 2011; Lansingh and Carter, 2009.

claim: A larger number of studies confirm the OA citation advantage compared to those that don't find it.
source: While some controlled studies have failed to find a difference in citations between OA and non-OA articles or attribute differences to factors other than access (Davis, 2011; Davis et al., 2008; Frandsen, 2009a; Gaulé and Maystre, 2011; Lansingh and Carter, 2009), a larger number of studies confirm the OA citation advantage.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the literature.

claim: Of 70 studies registered as of June 2016 in the SPARC Europe database, 46 (66%) found an OA citation advantage.
source: Of 70 studies registered as of June 2016 in the Scholarly Publishing and Academic Resources Coalition (SPARC) Europe database of citation studies, 46 (66%) found an OA citation advantage, 17 (24%) found no advantage, and 7 (10%) were inconclusive (SPARC Europe, 2016).
evidence: This is data from the SPARC Europe database as cited.

claim: Of 70 studies registered as of June 2016 in the SPARC Europe database, 17 (24%) found no OA citation advantage.
source: Of 70 studies registered as of June 2016 in the Scholarly Publishing and Academic Resources Coalition (SPARC) Europe database of citation studies, 46 (66%) found an OA citation advantage, 17 (24%) found no advantage, and 7 (10%) were inconclusive (SPARC Europe, 2016).
evidence: This is data from the SPARC Europe database as cited.

claim: Of 70 studies registered as of June 2016 in the SPARC Europe database, 7 (10%) were inconclusive regarding OA citation advantage.
source: Of 70 studies registered as of June 2016 in the Scholarly Publishing and Academic Resources Coalition (SPARC) Europe database of citation studies, 46 (66%) found an OA citation advantage, 17 (24%) found no advantage, and 7 (10%) were inconclusive (SPARC Europe, 2016).
evidence: This is data from the SPARC Europe database as cited.

claim: Numerical estimates of the OA citation advantage range from -5% to 600% according to one review.
source: Numerical estimates of the citation advantage in two reviews range from -5% to 600% (Swan, 2010) and 25% to 250% (Wagner, 2010).
evidence: This is from a review by Swan, 2010.

claim: Numerical estimates of the OA citation advantage range from 25% to 250% according to another review.
source: Numerical estimates of the citation advantage in two reviews range from -5% to 600% (Swan, 2010) and 25% to 250% (Wagner, 2010).
evidence: This is from a review by Wagner, 2010.

claim: The size of the OA citation advantage is often dependent on discipline.
source: The size of the advantage observed is often dependent on discipline (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1 which shows variation across disciplines.

claim: The OA citation advantage can be conferred regardless of whether articles are published in fully OA journals, hybrid journals, or self-archived in open repositories.
source: Importantly, the OA citation advantage can be conferred regardless of whether articles are published in fully OA journals, subscription journals with OA options (hybrid journals), or self-archived in open repositories (Eysenbach, 2006; Hajjem et al., 2006; Gargouri et al., 2010; Research Information Network, 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Swan, 2010; Wagner, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The OA citation advantage is not explained by selection bias in at least some cases.
source: Moreover, at least in some cases, the advantage is not explained by selection bias (i.e., authors deliberately posting their better work to open platforms), as openly archived articles receive a citation advantage regardless of whether archiving is initiated by the author or mandated by an institution or funder (Gargouri et al., 2010; Xia and Nakanishi, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gargouri et al., 2010 and Xia and Nakanishi, 2012.

claim: Openly archived articles receive a citation advantage regardless of whether archiving is initiated by the author or mandated by an institution or funder.
source: Moreover, at least in some cases, the advantage is not explained by selection bias (i.e., authors deliberately posting their better work to open platforms), as openly archived articles receive a citation advantage regardless of whether archiving is initiated by the author or mandated by an institution or funder (Gargouri et al., 2010; Xia and Nakanishi, 2012).
